title: L-SR1: Learned Symmetric-Rank-One Preconditioning
claim: On standard hard test landscapes, the projection-guided learned optimizer follows more direct, stable paths to the minimum than its ablated variant and classical baselines.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, contour plots with overlaid trajectories, shared legend in each panel
description: Three square contour-plot panels in a row, each showing a 2-D test function: (a) Rastrigin, (b) Rosenbrock, (c) Quadratic. Backgrounds are colored level sets: a noisy teal-yellow multi-modal pattern for Rastrigin, and a purple valley for Rosenbrock and the quadratic. Three optimizer paths are drawn with tick markers: LBFGS in yellow, LSR1 without projection in orange, and LSR1 with PGSM in dark red. A black dot marks the start and a black star marks the global minimum. In Rosenbrock and the quadratic, the dark red path reaches the star more directly. In Rastrigin the paths are erratic. Each panel has a semi-transparent legend in the lower right and a bold italic caption below. The eye goes first to the bright trajectories and the star.
caption: Optimization trajectories. Example trajectories of LBFGS, L-SR1 with PGSM, and L-SR1 without (No Prj.) on a quadratic function and two well-known challenging benchmark functions [ref]---the Rosenbrock and Rastrigin functions. PGSM improves the performance of L-SR1 compared to the variant without PGSM (No Prj.), while maintaining model compactness.
abstract: End-to-end deep learning has achieved impressive results but often relies on large labeled datasets, exhibits limited generalization to unseen scenarios, and incurs substantial computational cost. Classical optimization methods, in contrast, are more data-efficient and lightweight but frequently suffer from slow convergence. Learned optimizers aim to bridge this gap, yet existing approaches have focused primarily on first-order methods, while learned second-order optimization has received much less attention. We introduce L-SR1, a learned second-order optimizer inspired by the classical Symmetric Rank-One (SR1) method. At its core, L-SR1 employs a Projection-Guided Secant Mechanism (PGSM) that generates positive semi-definite preconditioners and biases meta-training toward the quasi-Newton secant relation. Through controlled analytic benchmarks, we study stability, generalization across problem dimensions, and search direction quality, and further evaluate L-SR1 on Monocular Human Mesh Recovery (HMR), where it outperforms both classical and learned optimization-based baselines. With a compact model and no reliance on task-specific fine-tuning or annotated data, L-SR1 demonstrates strong generalization and can be integrated into a broad range of iterative optimization problems to accelerate convergence and reduce the required number of iterations.
